changes.before: Working rules for selected cases: valency is combining capacity written here without sign; a monatomic ion's oxidation number equals its signed charge; an uncombined element has oxidation number0; H usually+1 and O usually−2 in the ordinary compounds here (exceptions exist). For NaCl,MgO,H2O,CO2,NH3, find named atoms' oxidation numbers using total0. For elementalO2 give O oxidation number. Explain why oxygen valency2 does not mean oxidation number+2 and why oxidation number need not be an actual ionic charge in a covalent molecule. Use common valencies:H1,O2,Na1,Mg2,Al3,Cl1 in these tasks. IUPAC oxidation-state guidance: https://iupac.org/recommendation/comprehensive-definition-of-oxidation-state/.
changes.after: Working rules for selected cases: valency is combining capacity written here without sign; a monatomic ion's oxidation number equals its signed charge; an uncombined element has oxidation number0; H usually+1 and O usually−2 in the ordinary compounds here (exceptions exist). For NaCl,MgO,H2O,CO2,NH3, find named atoms' oxidation numbers using total0. For elementalO2 give O oxidation number. Explain why oxygen valency2 does not mean oxidation number+2 and why oxidation number need not be an actual ionic charge in a covalent molecule. Use common valencies:H1,O2,Na1,Mg2,Al3,Cl1 in these tasks. IUPAC oxidation-state guidance: https://iupac.org/recommendation/comprehensive-definition-of-oxidation-state/. Finally use the supplied valencies to formulate sodium chloride and magnesium oxide from element symbols; show the simplest combining ratio instead of merely copying a supplied formula.

changes.before: NaCl:Na+1,Cl−1;MgO:Mg+2,O−2;H2O:H+1,O−2;CO2:C+4,O−2;NH3:N−3,H+1;O2:O0. Valency lacks the sign used in oxidation numbers here. CO2's assigned C+4 is formal bookkeeping, not a freeC4+ion. Hydrogen−1 in metal hydrides/peroxide oxygen−1 are beyond these worked cases but refute universal wording.
changes.after: NaCl:Na+1,Cl−1;MgO:Mg+2,O−2;H2O:H+1,O−2;CO2:C+4,O−2;NH3:N−3,H+1;O2:O0. Valency lacks the sign used in oxidation numbers here. CO2's assigned C+4 is formal bookkeeping, not a freeC4+ion. Hydrogen−1 in metal hydrides/peroxide oxygen−1 are beyond these worked cases but refute universal wording. Formulation:Na(valency1) withCl1 gives1:1,NaCl;Mg2 withO2 simplifies2:2 to1:1,MgO. This explicitly elicits compound formulation;it does not elicit an ion-formation description.
